info.text: Unit 26 — Handling ground damage and the damage report. Listening, reading, use of English, and vocabulary items keyed to the four dialogues and the taught bank terms.

name.text: L1 · Dialogue 1 — where is the dent

questiontext.text: Listen to Dialogue 1 again. Where does the mechanic say the dent is located?

generalfeedback.text: The mechanic gives the precise location: "zone 127, near station 480, directly below the forward cargo door." A professional report always fixes the damage by zone and station, never by a vague phrase like "lower left".

feedback.text: Correct — this is the exact zone and station the mechanic reports.
That is the location of the second dent, in Dialogue 3, not the first.
No zone 217 is mentioned. Listen again for the two numbers together.
The digits are close, but the mechanic says 127 and 480. Numbers must be caught exactly.

questiontext.text: Listen to Dialogue 1 again. The mechanic reports that nobody is injured.

generalfeedback.text: The mechanic says, "Nobody is injured, although a belt loader struck the fuselage." Checking for injuries is the first thing the lead asks, and the answer is that there are none.

feedback.text: Correct — the mechanic confirms nobody is injured.
Listen again: the mechanic clearly says nobody is injured.

questiontext.text: Listen to Dialogue 2 again. What dent depth, in millimetres, does the mechanic measure at the centre of the damage? (Write the number only.)

generalfeedback.text: The mechanic reads 1.4 millimetres at the centre. Because the flat-skin limit is 2.0 mm, this depth is within limits.

feedback.text: Correct — 1.4 mm, which is within the 2.0 mm flat-skin limit.

questiontext.text: Listen to Dialogue 2 again. The SRM states the depth for this flat panel must remain under how many millimetres? (Write the number only.)

generalfeedback.text: The lead reads the allowable damage limit: the depth must remain under 2 millimetres on this flat skin. The measured 1.4 mm is therefore within limits.

feedback.text: Correct — the flat-skin limit is 2 millimetres.
1 mm is the stricter limit that applies over a stringer or a frame, not on this flat panel.

questiontext.text: Listen to Dialogue 3 again. Why does the second dent need a referral, not a simple blend out?

generalfeedback.text: The dent is 2.6 mm against a 2 mm limit and it sits over a frame, in an area the SRM does not cover. Both facts — over a frame and out of limits — drive the referral to engineering.

answer.text: It sits over a frame and exceeds the limit.

feedback.text: Correct — over a frame and out of limits, so engineering must design the repair.

answer.text: It sits on flat skin and stays within the limit.

feedback.text: That describes the first dent in Dialogue 2, which was within limits.

answer.text: It is only a light scratch beside the stringer.

feedback.text: A light scratch can be blended out; this is a deep dent over a frame.

answer.text: It is a small dent that the SRM already covers.

feedback.text: The opposite is true: the SRM does not cover this frame area, so a referral is needed.

questiontext.text: Listen to Dialogue 3 again. The SRM provides a ready repair scheme for this frame area.

generalfeedback.text: The lead says the SRM has a scheme "for flat skin, but not for this frame area." Because the manual does not cover it, the damage must go to engineering as a referral.

feedback.text: Listen again: the SRM covers flat skin, but not this frame area.
Correct — the SRM does not cover the frame area, so a referral is raised.

questiontext.text: Listen to Dialogue 3 again. What is the dent depth, in millimetres, of the second dent? (Write the number only.)

generalfeedback.text: The second dent is 2.6 mm deep against a 2 mm limit, so it is out of limits. That figure, plus the frame location, is why the mechanic recommends a referral.

feedback.text: Correct — 2.6 mm, which is above the 2 mm limit.

questiontext.text:
Read this task-card extract, then answer.

TASK CARD 53-10-11 — FUSELAGE SKIN DENT INSPECTION
1. Clean the damaged area before you measure.
2. Measure the dent with a depth gauge at the deepest point.
3. Allowable dent depth on flat skin: 2.0 mm.
4. Allowable dent depth over a frame or a stringer: 1.0 mm.
5. Within limits: record it in the tech log and close the task.
6. Out of limits: raise a referral to Engineering. Do not blend out.

What is the allowable dent depth over a stringer?

generalfeedback.text: Line 4 sets the stricter limit of 1.0 mm over a frame or a stringer. The 2.0 mm figure in line 3 is for flat skin only.

feedback.text: Correct — line 4 gives 1.0 mm over a frame or a stringer.
2.0 mm is the flat-skin limit in line 3, not the stringer limit.
2.6 mm is a measured out-of-limits depth from the dialogues, not a card limit.
No 0.5 mm limit appears on the card. Re-read line 4.

questiontext.text: Using the same TASK CARD 53-10-11 above: the card allows you to blend out a dent that is out of limits.

generalfeedback.text: Line 6 says: out of limits — raise a referral, and "Do not blend out." Blending out is only for light, in-limits damage.

feedback.text: The card forbids it: "Do not blend out" an out-of-limits dent.
Correct — an out-of-limits dent must never be blended out; raise a referral.

name.text: R3 · Tech log — why out of limits

questiontext.text:
Read this tech-log entry, then answer.

TECH LOG — YL-AAB
Belt loader contact during pushback, Stand 5.
Dent in fuselage skin: zone 127, station 480, over a stringer.
Depth 1.4 mm, length 40 mm. No crack, no corrosion.
Stringer limit 1.0 mm — dent is OUT OF LIMITS. Aircraft on hold.
Referral raised to Engineering. Do not fit the cargo door panel.

Why is this dent out of limits?

generalfeedback.text: The dent is 1.4 mm deep but it sits over a stringer, where the limit is only 1.0 mm. The stricter stringer limit, not the 2.0 mm flat-skin limit, is what makes it out of limits.

answer.text: The depth is above the 1.0 mm stringer limit.

feedback.text: Correct — over a stringer the limit is 1.0 mm, and 1.4 mm exceeds it.

answer.text: The depth is below the 2.0 mm flat-skin limit.

feedback.text: Being below the flat-skin limit does not help: over a stringer the limit is stricter.

answer.text: There is fresh corrosion beside the damaged skin.

feedback.text: The entry states "No crack, no corrosion." The depth is the reason.

answer.text: The dent is longer than forty millimetres across.

feedback.text: Length is 40 mm and is not the limiting factor; depth over a stringer is.

questiontext.text: Using the same TECH LOG — YL-AAB entry above: staff are told not to fit the cargo door panel.

generalfeedback.text: The last line reads: "Do not fit the cargo door panel." The aircraft is on hold until engineering answers the referral.

feedback.text: Correct — the entry says the cargo door panel must not be fitted yet.
Re-read the last line: the cargo door panel must not be fitted.

name.text: R5 · Tech log — the action taken

questiontext.text: Using the same TECH LOG — YL-AAB entry above: what does the crew do because the dent is out of limits?

generalfeedback.text: Because the dent is out of limits, the crew raise a referral to engineering and place the aircraft on hold. They do not repair or close the entry themselves.

answer.text: They raise a referral to Engineering.

feedback.text: Correct — an out-of-limits dent goes to engineering as a referral.

answer.text: They blend out the dent and close the log.

feedback.text: You must never blend out an out-of-limits dent.

answer.text: They fit the cargo door panel straight away.

feedback.text: The entry forbids fitting the cargo door panel while on hold.

answer.text: They lower the allowable damage limit value.

feedback.text: Limits come from the SRM; a mechanic cannot lower them.

questiontext.text:
Write one word in the gap.

The mechanic ______ found the dent wrote the report.

generalfeedback.text: Use "who" for people. Latvian and Russian often use one relative word for people and things, so English "who" for a person needs care.

feedback.text: Correct — "who" is used for people.
"Which" is for things. A mechanic is a person, so use "who".
"That" is possible in speech, but the target here is "who" for a person.

questiontext.text:
Write one word in the gap.

The dent, ______ exceeds the limit, needs a referral.

generalfeedback.text: After a comma, adding extra information about one known dent, use "which" (never "that"). The commas signal a non-defining clause.

feedback.text: Correct — a non-defining clause after a comma uses "which".
"That" cannot follow a comma in a non-defining clause. Use "which".
"Who" is for people; a dent is a thing, so use "which".

questiontext.text:
Write one word in the gap.

This is the zone ______ the belt loader hit the skin.

generalfeedback.text: Use "where" for a place or a location, such as a zone or a stand.

feedback.text: Correct — "where" points to a place, here the zone.
"Which" is possible with a preposition, but the single-word target for a place is "where".
"Who" is for people, not a location. Use "where".

name.text: U4 · Combine with a relative clause

questiontext.text:
Join the two sentences. Write the one relative word that fills the gap.

The dent sits over a frame. It needs a referral.

The dent ______ sits over a frame needs a referral.

generalfeedback.text: Here the clause identifies which dent you mean, with no commas — a defining clause. Both "that" and "which" are acceptable for a thing in a defining clause.

feedback.text: Correct — a defining clause about a thing takes "that" (or "which").
Also correct — "which" works in a defining clause with no comma.
"Who" is for people; a dent is a thing, so use "that" or "which".

questiontext.text:
Write the one bank word for the meaning in brackets.

We send a difficult case to engineering for a decision. This action is a ______. (one word)

generalfeedback.text: A referral is the action of sending a difficult case to engineering for a decision, used when the SRM does not cover the damage.

feedback.text: Correct — a referral goes to engineering for a decision.
Correct — "referral" is the term.
A repair scheme is the approved plan to fix damage; the action of sending it is a referral.

questiontext.text:
Write the one bank word for the meaning in brackets.

Metal damage from a chemical reaction, similar to rust, is called ______. (one word)

generalfeedback.text: Corrosion is chemical metal damage, like rust. Corrosion near a dent changes the whole repair scheme, so inspectors always check for it.

feedback.text: Correct — corrosion is chemical, rust-like metal damage.
A crack is a split in the metal, not chemical damage. The word here is corrosion.
A scratch is a thin surface mark, not chemical damage. The word here is corrosion.

questiontext.text:
In Simplified Technical English (STE) we choose a common, approved word. Replace the long word with the approved everyday verb.

"Commence the inspection" → "______ the inspection." (one word)

generalfeedback.text: STE prefers plain, approved verbs: "start" (or "begin") instead of "commence". Short approved words reduce misunderstanding between readers from different countries.

feedback.text: Correct — STE uses the plain verb "start".
Also accepted — "begin" is a plain, approved verb.
"Initiate" is another long word STE avoids. Use "start".

questiontext.text:
Write the two-word bank phrase for the meaning in brackets.

A dent whose depth is inside the maximum the manual allows is ______ ______. (two words)

generalfeedback.text: "Within limits" means the damage is inside the maximum the SRM allows, so no repair is needed and the aircraft can return to service.

feedback.text: Correct — "within limits" means inside the allowed maximum.
That is the opposite: "out of limits" means the damage exceeds the allowed maximum.

questiontext.text: Match each structural term with its plain meaning.

generalfeedback.text: Dent = a smooth hollow from an impact; stringer = a lengthwise stiffener; frame = a curved ring giving the fuselage its shape; referral = sending a case to engineering; corrosion = rust-like chemical damage.

answer.text: a smooth hollow pushed into the metal skin
a long strip that stiffens the skin from inside
a curved ring that shapes the fuselage
sending a difficult case to engineering

name.text: V2 · Match term to meaning (damage and tools)

questiontext.text: Match each term with its plain meaning.

generalfeedback.text: Skin = the outer metal panels; gouge = a deeper mark removing more metal; scratch = a thin surface mark; blend out = smooth away light damage by sanding; depth gauge = the tool that measures how deep a dent is.

answer.text: the outer metal panels of the aircraft
a deeper mark that removes more metal
a thin mark on the surface
smooth away light damage by sanding
the tool that measures how deep a dent is

questiontext.text: Which is the correct English name for the manual's maximum permitted damage?

generalfeedback.text: The fixed collocation is "allowable damage limit" — singular "damage", singular "limit", with the adjective "allowable". The other forms mix up plurals and word forms.

feedback.text: Correct — this is the fixed technical collocation.
"Allowance" is a noun; the term needs the adjective "allowable" and singular "limit".
"Damage" is uncountable here and "limit" is singular in this collocation.
"Allowing" and "damaged" are the wrong word forms for this fixed term.

questiontext.text: Which word means "directly next to; right beside"?

generalfeedback.text: "Adjacent" means directly next to something. In the dialogues a stringer runs adjacent to the dent, so it must be inspected too.

feedback.text: Correct — "adjacent" means right beside.
"Ascending" means rising or going up, not next to.
"Adequate" means good enough, not next to.
"Abundant" means plentiful, not next to.
